html:
Hopewell is the name archaeologists give to a network of cultures in the Ohio and Illinois valleys, from about 100 BCE to 500 CE. The map places the label in southern Ohio, its core area, though by 1492 the Hopewell world had been gone for a thousand years.

The Hopewell built huge earthworks: circles, squares and long walls of earth, some lined up with the moon, and burial mounds filled with fine goods. Those goods came from far away along trade routes: copper from Lake Superior, mica from the Appalachians, shells from the Gulf coast and obsidian from the Rocky Mountains. They grew native seed crops of the Eastern Agricultural Complex as well as hunting and gathering.

Hopewell followed the earlier Adena culture and faded around 500 CE. The Hopewell Culture page covers it in its own years; the later Mississippian towns built mounds of their own. Eight Ohio earthwork sites became a World Heritage Site in 2023.
